body:
What an SEO services contract contains and how to check what you receive month by month. A well-drafted SEO services contract does not promise guaranteed rankings, but describes exactly which activities are carried out, how often and who is responsible for each part of the collaboration.

Many misunderstandings between an agency and a client arise not from poor results, but from vague clauses signed in haste. A clear contract prevents this type of conflict from the very first month of working together.

What an SEO services contract contains and how to check what you receive month by month

An SEO services contract is not a formality signed once and forgotten in a drawer. It remains the document you return to whenever you want to check that you are receiving exactly what you paid for.

The sections below show, clause by clause, what you should find in any serious SEO optimization contract and which checks you can make monthly without relying solely on the agency's word.

Why clear clauses matter in an SEO services contract

SEO is an activity whose results appear over time, not immediately after the first invoice. That is precisely why, without clear clauses, any weaker month can be interpreted either as an agency failure or as normal variation, depending on who explains the situation.

A detailed contract moves the discussion from emotional ground to verifiable ground. Instead of "I don't see results", the client can say "last month's report showed five articles published, but only three actually appeared".

This precision protects both parties. The agency can demonstrate its work with documents, and the client can request specific corrections rather than a hasty termination over an issue that could have been resolved through a conversation.

The difference is clearest when renewing the contract. A client who can show exactly what they received, month by month, negotiates renewal from an informed position, rather than on the basis of a general impression of satisfaction or dissatisfaction. The agency, in turn, can justify a request for a larger budget with a specific list of additional activities, rather than vague wording about "expanding the strategy".

The list of included work: what must be in black and white

The most common source of disputes is a vaguely worded list of work, such as "ongoing optimization" or "monthly SEO activities". The contract must name the specific activities and their frequency.

Technical and content activities

For the technical and content aspects, the contract should specify the number of articles published monthly, an initial SEO audit with a clear delivery deadline and the frequency of subsequent technical fixes.

  • The number of articles or pages optimized per month, with subjects agreed in advance or proposed for approval.
  • An initial technical audit, with a list of issues and a deadline for fixing each one.
  • Recurring technical fixes: loading speed, crawl errors, structured data.
  • Optimization of meta titles and descriptions for the pages targeted that month.

Links and external authority

If the package also includes link building services, the contract must specify an estimated number of links per month and the types of sources targeted, not just the phrase "authority growth".

  • The approximate number of new links obtained monthly and the target domains, whether general or niche.
  • An explicit ban on using low-quality link networks that can attract penalties.
  • How acquired links are reported: URL, source and anchor text used.

Reporting: what the contract must stipulate about results

The contract must establish both that there is a report and what it contains, how often the client receives it and who explains it. A report sent by email without any discussion leaves room for misinterpretation.

The reporting clause should provide the client with direct access to Google Search Console and Google Analytics, not just screenshots selected by the agency. Direct access to the data is the only real guarantee that the report reflects the full situation, not just the favorable part.

The standard frequency is monthly, with a written summary and, optionally, a short presentation call. The contract can also specify a fixed delivery deadline, for example, within the first five working days of the following month.

The report's minimum contents are also worth specifying explicitly in the contract, so they do not depend on goodwill in any particular month:

  • A list of work actually completed, with dates and, where applicable, verifiable URLs.
  • Changes in organic traffic and rankings for the keywords agreed together at the start of the collaboration.
  • Technical issues found and the status of their resolution, not just those already closed.
  • A short plan for the following month, so activities remain predictable for the client.

Ownership of accounts and data: an often overlooked clause

One of the most important clauses, and one of the most frequently omitted, establishes who actually owns the accounts used in the campaign. Without this clarification, a client can lose access to their own data if they change agencies.

  • The Google Search Console and Google Analytics accounts are created using the client's email address, not the agency's.
  • Administrator access to the site and hosting panel remains with the client, while the agency receives a limited role sufficient for the contracted work.
  • The domain and hosting are registered in the client's name, regardless of who makes payments on their behalf.
  • When the contract ends, the client retains access to all accounts and historical data without additional conditions.

This clause seems like a formality until the collaboration ends abruptly. A contract that does not mention it leaves the client dependent on the agency's goodwill for their own data.

Why no serious contract promises guaranteed rankings

A clause promising a specific position in Google, for example "first position in three months", is a warning sign, not a commercial advantage. No agency controls Google's ranking algorithm, and a promise of this kind cannot be supported technically.

Google itself explicitly warns about this: using a third-party service or tool does not guarantee ranking success, and any ranking prediction remains the provider's estimate, not a certainty.

  • Promises of a fixed position ("guaranteed number 1") within a precise time frame.
  • Refusal to provide access to Search Console or Analytics under the pretext of a "proprietary method".
  • Reports with keywords unrelated to the client's actual business activities.
  • Contracts with no termination clause or with disproportionate penalties for the client.

A fair contract talks about activities, deadlines and transparency, not guarantees that nobody can fully control.

Contract duration, termination and the notice period

SEO needs a few months to show clear trends, so most serious contracts have a minimum duration of three to six months. A shorter duration does not allow time for activities to produce a visible effect.

The contract should also establish a reasonable notice period for termination, usually thirty days, plus the agency's obligation to hand over all materials produced: articles, lists of acquired links and technical documentation.

Termination penalties, if any, must be proportional to the work already performed, not a fixed sum intended to discourage the client from leaving regardless of the reason.

An often omitted aspect is the actual handover at the end of the collaboration. The contract should specify a concrete deadline for transferring passwords and administrator rights, as well as a written inventory of published articles, acquired links and technical changes applied to the site. Without this inventory, changing agencies means reconstructing the history of the work from memory.

How to check what you receive month by month: a short checklist

The monthly check does not have to be complicated. A few direct comparisons between the contract and the report received quickly show whether things are going as agreed.

  • Amount of work: compare the published articles and reported technical fixes with the number agreed in the contract.
  • Data access: check for yourself, directly in Search Console and Analytics, not just through screenshots sent by the agency.
  • Independent results: run your own technical check, for example with GOAI site analyzer, and compare it with the issues marked as resolved in the report.
  • Reporting consistency: note whether the report arrives by the contractual deadline or is delayed without explanation.
  • Verifiable evidence: ask for the exact URLs of new links and published articles, not just aggregate figures.

If one of these checks shows a consistent discrepancy from the contract, the discussion with the agency must start from the signed document, not general impressions about traffic.

What you can check before signing

Before signing, it is worth asking for a list of previous projects. A real project portfolio with verifiable examples says more about an agency than any promise written in a proposal.

It is also worth comparing two or three proposals for the same objective to see whether their lists of work and data ownership clauses are similar. A proposal far below market price usually hides a thinner list of work, not unusual efficiency.

A few direct questions asked before signing quickly reveal differences between proposals:

  • Who remains the owner of the Search Console and Analytics accounts and the domain throughout the collaboration.
  • What happens to articles already published if one party decides to end the contract early.
  • How long the notice period is and which handover obligations remain in force after the final invoice.

A well-written SEO services contract remains simple to read and easy to check month by month, without hidden clauses or promises nobody can guarantee.
